name: Vector Compression (Scalar, Product and Binary Quantisation)
question: Can the index fit in a fraction of the RAM?
summary: Vector compression stores fewer bits per dimension so a large index fits in RAM. Scalar quantisation maps each float32 to an int8 (4× smaller); product quantisation (PQ) splits the vector into sub-vectors and stores a one-byte codebook id for each (often 32–64× smaller); binary quantisation keeps only the sign of each dimension (32× smaller). Each step down loses some recall, which is won back by oversampling candidates from the compressed codes and rescoring them with full-precision vectors kept on SSD. This technique is about bytes per dimension; reducing the number of dimensions is covered in module 4, and multi-stage pipelines in general by Layered Approximate Search.
useCases: Corpora of crores of vectors where float32 would need hundreds of GB of RAM
Cutting the monthly bill of a managed vector database
Fast first-stage candidates before a precise rescore

items.detail: 4× smaller; each dimension clipped to a range and mapped to 256 levels; recall loss usually about 1–2 points
vector split into m sub-vectors, each stored as a codebook id; needs training; 16–64× smaller
1 bit per dimension, 32× smaller, Hamming distance is very fast; works best on 1,000+ dims from models trained for it
fetch k × factor candidates from the compressed index, e.g. 40 for a top 10
re-rank candidates with original vectors, often read from SSD
recall at k against exact float32 search on your own queries

steps: Measure RAM, latency and recall at 10 with float32 as the baseline
Pick the encoding: int8 first, binary or PQ when RAM is the binding limit
Keep original vectors on SSD and rescore an oversampled candidate set
Tune the oversampling factor until recall is back within a point of the baseline
pitfalls: Binary quantisation on a small or unsuited embedding model, where recall collapses
Compressing without keeping the original vectors, so rescoring is impossible
Reporting speed-ups without measuring recall against exact search
remember: Fewer bits in RAM, full vectors on disk, oversample and rescore.

steps.title: Size the problem
steps.text: Bazaar Kart, a fictional marketplace, has 2 crore product vectors of 1,024 dims. As float32 that is 2 crore × 4,096 bytes = 81.9 GB of RAM, about ₹49,140 a month at ₹600 per GB-month.

steps.title: Choose the encoding
steps.text: int8 cuts it 4× to 20.5 GB. Binary keeps one bit per dimension: 128 bytes a vector, 2.6 GB in RAM. PQ with 64 one-byte codes would be 1.3 GB but needs training.

steps.title: Keep the originals on SSD
steps.text: The float32 vectors stay on disk. They are not searched; they are read only for the few candidates that need a precise score.

steps.title: Rescore
steps.text: The compressed index finds candidates with fast Hamming distance, then each candidate is re-ranked with its float32 vector.

steps.title: Oversample
steps.text: Fetching 4 × 10 = 40 candidates gives the rescoring step room to fix the order and recover near misses.

steps.title: Measure recall
steps.text: Against exact search on 1,000 real queries, binary alone finds 74% of the true top 10; with rescoring at ×4 it finds 96%, in 13 ms instead of 40 ms.

pros: 4× to 64× less RAM, often the largest cost of a vector database
Faster distance computation, especially Hamming on binary codes
Rescoring recovers most lost recall cheaply
Supported natively by most vector stores
cons: PQ needs training and retraining when data drifts
Binary suits only some embedding models and high dimensions
Keeping originals for rescoring still needs disk
avoidWhen: Small indexes that already fit in RAM comfortably
Models with few dimensions (under about 512) for binary quantisation

practice.scenario: Bazaar Kart, a fictional marketplace, holds 2 crore product vectors of 1,024 dims. As float32 they need 81.9 GB of RAM, about ₹49,140 a month. It stores binary codes in RAM (2.6 GB), keeps the float32 vectors on SSD, fetches 40 candidates for each top 10 and rescores them. Recall at 10 against exact search is 96%, and the RAM bill falls by about 95%.

industries.use: Crores of product and image vectors for search and recommendations
Transaction and document embeddings kept for years under retention rules
Call-note and ticket embeddings across many regions and languages

practice.analogy: Keeping a thumbnail of every photo in your pocket and fetching the full-size print only for the few that look right.

library.name: Sentence Transformers
library.what: quantize_embeddings turns float32 embeddings into int8 or packed binary before you store them.

practice.note: The model name is an example; binary works best with models of 1,000 or more dimensions. The recall check compares against exact float32 search on the same queries.

samples.code:
import numpy as np, faiss
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.quantization import quantize_embeddings

model = SentenceTransformer("mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1")
docs = [line.strip() for line in open("products.txt", encoding="utf-8")]
queries = [line.strip() for line in open("queries.txt", encoding="utf-8")]
d = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)
q = model.encode(queries, normalize_embeddings=True)

exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d.shape[1]); exact.add(d)
_, truth = exact.search(q, 10)

bits = quantize_embeddings(d, precision="ubinary")
binary = faiss.IndexBinaryFlat(d.shape[1]); binary.add(bits)
_, cand = binary.search(quantize_embeddings(q, precision="ubinary"), 40)

hits = 0
for i, c in enumerate(cand):
    top = c[np.argsort(-(d[c] @ q[i]))[:10]]      # rescore with float32
    hits += len(set(top) & set(truth[i]))
print("recall@10 after rescoring:", hits / (10 * len(queries)))
print("bytes per vector:", bits.shape[1], "vs", d.shape[1] * 4)

numericDrill.question: 2 crore vectors of 1,024 dims are stored as binary codes (1 bit per dimension). How many GB of RAM do the codes need?
numericDrill.answer: 1,024 bits = 128 bytes per vector. 2 crore × 128 bytes = 2,56,00,00,000 bytes ≈ 2.56 GB, against 81.9 GB for float32.

interview.question: How does product quantisation work?
interview.answer: The vector is split into m sub-vectors. For each sub-space a codebook of 256 centroids is trained, and each sub-vector is stored as the one-byte id of its nearest centroid. Distances are approximated from lookup tables.

interview.question: How do you win back recall after binary quantisation?
interview.answer: Oversample, for example fetch 40 candidates for a top 10 from the binary index, then rescore them with the original float32 vectors, which can live on SSD.
